---
title: "Household extremes, step by step"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`weather_extremes()` is a chain of step functions. This article runs the chain
one step at a time, so each step can be inspected and changed. Each table
carries its context to the next step: once the raster is read, its variable,
unit and dates travel with the data, and no later step asks for them again.

```{r setup}
library(c4e)
```

## The survey

The households need coordinates and an interview date. `prepare_coord()`
keeps one row per household and gives each distinct location an identifier
built from its coordinates, so the same place gets the same identifier in
every wave and file.

```{r survey}
survey <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "survey.csv", package = "c4e"))
survey$interview <- as.Date(survey$interview)

coord <- prepare_coord(survey, lat_var = lat, lon_var = lon,
                       id = hhid, interview = interview)
head(coord, 4)
```

`georef_coord()` turns the distinct locations into points. The coordinate
columns and their reference system come from the table; the assumption of
longitude and latitude in WGS84 is announced.

```{r points}
points <- georef_coord(coord)
points
```

## The climate data

`read_climate()` reads a raster with its dates, variable and unit, from the
file or from the conventions of common sources (ERA5, CHIRPS, WFDE5).

```{r read}
tmax <- read_climate(system.file("extdata", "tmax_daily.tif", package = "c4e"))
raster_meta(tmax)[c("variable", "unit", "time_step", "date_range")]
```

The thresholds below are in Celsius, so the raster is converted first.
`convert_unit()` knows the usual conversions (kelvin and Celsius, metres
and millimetres, rates per second and per day) and records the new unit.

```{r convert}
tmax <- convert_unit(tmax, "C")
```

## Extraction

`extract_by_coord()` reads the value of each day at each location: one row
per location, one column per day. Locations outside the raster, or on cells
missing in every layer, are reported.

```{r extract}
extracted <- extract_by_coord(tmax, points)
extracted[1:3, 1:6]
```

## Daily indicators

`calc_threshold_day()` flags the days beyond each threshold and records how
far beyond they are. The table becomes long, one row per location and day,
and every new column is registered with what it measures.

```{r thresholds}
days <- calc_threshold_day(extracted, above = c(30, 35))
days[1:3, ]
```

The unit was not typed: it came from the table. `calc_spell()` then finds
the runs of flagged days. It needs no argument either; it follows every
flag that is registered, and takes two days as the shortest spell.

```{r spells}
spells <- calc_spell(days)
dplyr::filter(spells, !is.na(spell_abv_30)) |> head(3)
```

## Summaries before each interview

`summarise_by_interview()` sums the flagged days and summarises the spells
(longest, mean, total, number) over a window before each household's
interview. The window is an object: here the year before the interview and
the year before that.

```{r summary}
summary <- summarise_by_interview(coord, spells,
                                  window = window_lag("1 year", n_lags = 1))
print(summary, n = 4)
```

Other windows are a season (`window_season(6, 9)` for June to September),
a fixed period (`window_fixed()`) or the time since an event
(`window_since()`). A window short of data gives a missing value rather than
a zero: `min_coverage` sets the share of days that must be present.

## What the table knows

The table keeps the steps that produced it and what every column means.
`c4e_labels()` writes a label for each column from that context, which
`write_stata()` uses:

```{r context}
c4e_history(summary)
c4e_labels(summary)[c("day_abv_30_sum", "spell_abv_35_max")]
```

```{r stata}
write_stata(summary, file.path(tempdir(), "household_extremes.dta"))
```

`validate_c4e()` checks a table for duplicate rows, empty indicators, units
without data and gaps in the dates:

```{r validate}
validate_c4e(summary)
```
